items.title: Research Tools: University of Richmond Distant Viewing Lab Releases DataReel, a New AI Tool for Film Research
items.raw_text: From the University of Richmond: University of Richmond’s Distant Viewing Lab has released DataReel , a new open access, AI-powered tool that helps researchers analyze films. DataReel uses AI models to automatically capture data from over 2,000 films, presenting it in an interactive, visual format. It measures descriptions of scenes, the characters onscreen, shot length, framing distance (close-ups or long shots), how many people are on screen, how much the camera moves, and how much of the film is speech or music. The patterns could help scholars explore questions such as how close-ups influence psychological engagement, how pacing affects narrative tension, and how visual and audio techniques vary across genres. The Distant Viewing Lab is directed by Taylor Arnold, professor of data science and statistics, and Lauren Tilton, professor of digital humanities and director of UR’s Center for Liberal Arts and AI. “Current AI models can analyze two-dimensional images, but not how or why they were filmed in a particular way,” said Tilton. “Our research will further the ability of AI not only to recognize objects in moving images but also to analyze patterns, an important step forward for all scholarly communities working with digital media.” Support for this project was awarded by Schmidt Sciences and includes collaboration with UC Berkeley and Bowdoin College. items.title: Dr. Carla Hayden: “The Future of Libraries is About More Than Books”
items.raw_text: From a New Op/Ed by Dr. Carla Hayden on Time Magazine/Time.com: Dr. Carla Hayden Historically, libraries have served as a crucial part of the cultural and civic infrastructure of the nation, responding to local needs and bringing the world to people of all ages. However, in many places today, libraries and library workers are under attack . These attacks are echoes of the past, yet contain a new intensity when libraries are one of the only places where people can go for accurate information and inspiration, while also providing an all-important and free-of-cost “ third space ” between work and home. As the 14th Librarian of Congress, as a Senior Fellow at Mellon, and as a librarian whose career spans several decades among various types of libraries, I’ve had the opportunity to work and engage with library workers in all positions. One thing that becomes clear when you talk to librarians today is that libraries must embed themselves in the community, and the community in them. The institutions that will survive are the ones that let their communities shape them. Across fields, library and cultural workers are taking stock of local experts and leaders, leveraging their libraries as a convener and curator of their local community and its residents. items.title: AI is Reshaping the Role of Academic Librarians; Elsevier Releases Librarian of the Future Report
items.raw_text: From an Elsevier News Release: Today, Elsevier shares findings from its global Librarian of the Future research, revealing how artificial intelligence (AI) and changing research needs are reshaping the role of academic librarians. Drawing on insights from 1,100 academic librarians across 88 countries, alongside interviews with researchers and academic leaders, the report reveals a profession harnessing AI while also anticipating a greater role in helping institutions navigate its risks. The findings point to an opportunity for librarians to become more closely involved in institutional decision-making and strengthen their position as strategic partners in research. [Clip] Librarians expect their role in AI to grow meaningfully. Almost all (95%) expect demand for AI support to increase over the next five years, while 82% believe librarians should lead AI literacy initiatives for researchers and 76% believe they should play a role in AI governance. Source: Librarian of the Future Report (2026) While librarians are ready to contribute to AI initiatives, only 30% report their institution has implemented an AI policy. These findings highlight a potential gap between the pace of AI adoption and institutional preparedness. With this in mind, the report points to an increasingly important role for librarians in helping researchers navigate trusted information, responsible AI use and research integrity. Source: Librarian of the Future Report (2026) Jim O’Donnell, University Librarian

items.raw_text: From The Salt Lake Tribune: The Republican representative behind Utah’s statewide school book ban law was ousted last week. Rep. Ken Ivory, R-West Jordan, lost his race against Democrat Drew Howells, who secured 58.11% of the vote as of Friday morning. Ivory received about 41.89%. He acknowledged the defeat in a recent Facebook post. Two years ago, Ivory sponsored Utah’s sensitive materials law. It requires a book to be removed from all public schools in the state if at least three school districts (or at least two districts and five charter schools) determine it amounts to “objective sensitive material” — pornographic or otherwise indecent content, as defined by state code. [Clip] Since then, a total of 44 books have been banned from all Utah public schools. Once a title lands on the list, school districts must destroy all copies. Davis is home to a prominent book ban advocate, Brooke Stephens, who shares a connection with Ivory. items.title: Scaffolding Early Literacy Learning During Public Library Storytime
items.raw_text: Public library storytimes are more than just a fun time for children; beneath the read-alouds, singing songs, fingerplays, bubbles, and movement activities, storytimes are packed with abundant opportunities that support children’s literacy learning [1]. We all know intentionality is a key ingredient to promote learning in storytime [2]. One way to do this is by incorporating the Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) [3], an educational theory by Lev Vygotsky, into storytime planning and design. With a little bit of foreplanning, we can structure literacy experiences to align with children’s developmental levels—the perfect spot for learning—neither too easy nor too challenging. This article provides an introduction and practical tips for storytime providers on how to intentionally scaffold learning during picture book reading in storytime using the ZPD. The Zone of Proximal Development So what exactly is the Zone of Proximal Development? The ZPD, as explained by Vygotsky, is the gap between what children can do alone and what children can do with the guidance of more knowledgeable others (Vygotsky et al., 1978). Think of it as a linear continuum. There are three different learning levels. Imagine that at one end of the continuum is a task children can perform independently. At the other end of the continuum is a task children cannot perform, even with help. And in the middle of the continuum is the ZPD, in which children can perform the task with guidance and support. A Quick E-Rate Refresher One of four programs within the FCC’s Universal Service Fund, set up in the 1996 Telecommunications Act, the E-Rate program was established to ensure public libraries and K-12 schools have affordable access to advanced telecommunications (i.e., broadband and internet access). According to the 2024 Annual Survey of Museum-Goers from the American Alliance of Museums and Wilkening Consulting, museum admission costs vary widely, from a few dollars to $40–$50 per adult at some institutions. Among U.S. adults who visit museums at least occasionally, cost was the number one barrier to visiting more often. Among frequent museum-goers, younger adults were twice as likely as seniors to be concerned about admission costs. In response to those barriers, and in an effort to enrich and inspire customers of all ages, many library systems have stepped up to provide access to art in a variety of forms. items.raw_text: Autism acceptance efforts have come a long way in recent years, and libraries are one of the key reasons why. As a librarian and the mother of two sons with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), I’ve witnessed this progress firsthand. In my capacity as the assistant director of the Beals Memorial Library (BML), I’ve seen how efforts to create more inclusive programs, services, and spaces can promote positive social change that dra-matically improves people’s quality of life, disabled or not. Through our “See Beyond the Spectrum” initiative, in recent years, BML has established new ASD-friendly programs, made our existing programs more accessible, updated our collections with texts by autistic writers, and established an autism caregiver support group. Our staff have gone through autism awareness training, and we’ve established partnerships with local organizations that serve autistic youth. Much of this workhas been supported by external grants, including generous funding from the ALA’s “Libraries Transforming Communities” initiative, which seeks to help libraries become more accessible to patrons with disabilities. Everything we’ve done has proved beneficial, both inside and outside of the library. Staff-patron interactions are more productive and less awkward. items.title: The Librarian’s New Role: Knowledge Discovery
items.raw_text: For more than thirty years I have been interested in one deceptively simple question: How do we find things? At first glance, the answer appears obvious. We search. But anyone who has spent a lifetime in libraries knows that searching and finding are not the same thing. Throughout my earlier articles in Public Libraries Online , I explored several aspects of this process. In Finding Answers , I argued that patrons rarely come looking for information; they come looking for answers. In Search vs. Research , I suggested that locating information is only the beginning of inquiry. In Keeping Things Found , I examined what happens after discovery, how knowledge is preserved, organized, and made retrievable for future use. Artificial intelligence is now transforming how people search and, perhaps more importantly, how they find. For the first time in history, millions of people no longer begin by opening a directory, consulting an index, or scanning pages of search results. Instead, they ask a question in ordinary language and receive what appears to be a finished answer. This is more than another improvement in search technology. It represents a fundamental change in the relationship between people and information. The question librarians should be asking is not whether artificial intelligence can answer questions. It clearly can. The more important question is this: What happens to the process of finding? Some have suggested that artificial intelligence will replace librarians. Hi

items.title: How Library Science Principles Power Community AI Literacy
items.raw_text: Public libraries are dealing with budget cuts, book bans, and the usual existential questions about whether anyone needs physical collections when they can google everything. And now AI shows up, and everyone assumes libraries are about to get steamrolled by it too. But watch what’s happening at reference desks across the country. Patrons ask how to determine whether an IRS email is real or a phishing attempt generated by AI. Small business owners are trying to figure out which AI tool won’t steal their marketing copy. Retired community members want to use AI to parse dense municipal documents but do not know where to start. A parent is concerned about their teenager using AI for homework and whether that’s cheating. These aren’t edge cases. This is what reference work looks like now. Much has been written about how libraries can use AI tools internally—chatbots for reference, algorithms for cataloging, and predictive analytics for collection development. But there’s another question we need to answer: How do libraries help communities navigate AI? And here’s what I realized while building AI governance frameworks: these are not computer science problems. They’re library science problems—questions about provenance, access, evaluation, and trust. The exact questions libraries have been answering for over a century, just dressed up in a new syntax. items.title: Tag! You’re It: RFID’s Big Play in Public Libraries
items.raw_text: Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) technology has become one of the most influential innovations shaping the future of library operations. Since its introduction into library settings in the late 1990s, RFID has steadily evolved from an experimental enhancement to a widely adopted tool for improving circulation, inventory management, and patron experience. As libraries continue to modernize and adapt to changing user expectations, understanding RFID, including its capabilities, limitations, and long-term implications, is essential for informed decision-making. This article provides a thorough overview of RFID technology in libraries, synthesizing research, case studies, and industry standards to help public librarians evaluate whether RFID is the right investment for their institutions. Understanding RFID Technology in Libraries RFID tags come in two primary forms: active and passive. Libraries exclusively use passive tags, which do not require an internal power source and are small enough to be concealed within books and media cases. Passive tags contain information that is picked up by a scanner, while active tags emit their own signals. In library settings, RFID tags store essential item information like title, author, call number, and location and can be read without direct line-of-sight. items.title: Making the Invisible Visible: Advocacy at the Heart of Public Libraries
items.raw_text: Public libraries face no shortage of challenges today. Ongoing censorship efforts, increasing threats to staff safety, growing public distrust of institutions, and rapid technological change continue to reshape the work of libraries and the people who sustain them. In this environment, advocacy matters more than ever. That message came through clearly at the 2026 Public Library Association conference, where many sessions focused on helping librarians strengthen their advocacy skills. At the heart of every library are the workers who understand its value best and are often its strongest advocates. One session I attended, “Advocacy at the Core of ALA’s Next 150 Years,” featured Sam Helmick, Maria McCauley, Daniel Montgomery, and Lisa Varga. The panel offered practical strategies for advocacy, including using easy digital tools to contact legislators, participating in National Library Legislative Day, supporting legislation such as the Right to Read Act, and inviting elected officials into library spaces to see the work firsthand. Another standout session, “Advocacy Strategies for Getting Things Done,” featured Lisa Wells, Amanda Kordeliski, Tim Miller, Gail Oehler, and Kelly Sitzman from libraries across Oklahoma. items.title: Creating Meaningful Connections Through Memory Cafés
items.raw_text: The 2026 Public Library Association conference featured many excellent sessions focused on programming and community engagement, but one that especially resonated with me was “Memory Cafés in Libraries: Creating Meaningful Connections,” presented by Christina M. Johnson, Allan M. Kleiman, and Susan H. McFadden. Before attending this session, I had heard of Memory Cafés but did not fully understand what they were, who they served, or how they could be integrated into library programming. By the end of the hour, I felt equipped with the knowledge and resources needed to successfully bring this type of program to my own library. The library where I work is within walking distance of two senior living apartment buildings, and our community of 16,000 is also home to several assisted living facilities. Older adults often make up the majority of attendees at our programs, so as the staff member responsible for adult programming, I attended PLA hoping to learn about meaningful services for this audience. The session began by defining the core audience for a Memory Café: people living with dementia, whether formally diagnosed or not, their caregivers, and volunteers interested in learning more. items.title: From Skeptic to Troublemaker: One Book Club Idea That Changed My Mind
items.raw_text: I’ll admit it: library book clubs make me instantly wary. People constantly ask libraries to offer them, only to never actually show up. And a book club for kids? Forget about it. They already have plenty of assigned reading at school. So when I attended Tanvi Rastogi’s session, “Speak Up: Using Middle Grade Books to Build Allyship Muscles,” I assumed it would be a low-stakes hour to slowly wake up and drink my coffee. items.title: “I Wanted To Write Something That Felt More Like A Hug” – DeAndra Davis On Her Enchanting Coming-Of-Age Novel
items.raw_text: Despite being smart, funny, and her class’s valedictorian, Jaliya has spent much of her high school career ignored by her classmates. After graduation, her dad encourages her to leave their South Florida home to spend the summer in Jamaica with her family, who she hasn’t seen in several years. Although reluctant to do so, Jaliya changes her mind after receiving an unsigned letter postmarked from Jamaica asking when she’s going to return there. Convinced the letter is from her estranged mother, Jaliya devises a plan to return to Jamaica, find her mother, and figure out once and for all why she left their family long ago. Yet once she’s back in Jamaica, Jaliya’s life grows unexpectedly richer.
